unitDescription.value: In this unit, students investigate the principles of user-centred design by creating a Minecraft modification or gameplay experience for a specific audience. Students work with stakeholders to identify needs, define design criteria, and develop user stories that guide the design process. They generate, prototype, communicate, and evaluate multiple design ideas before refining a solution that enhances the Minecraft experience for their target users. Students use emerging digital tools, including artificial intelligence where appropriate, to develop interactive content and communicate their designs. Throughout the unit, students apply agile project management practices to plan, monitor, and evaluate their work while considering future opportunities, user feedback, and the broader impact of their solutions.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: The Years 9–10 cohort consists of a diverse group of boys with a wide range of digital competencies, from students with strong technical skills and personal interest in IT, to those who require further support to confidently engage with digital systems. Many students come from regional or rural backgrounds, where access to structured digital learning opportunities may have been limited. The program is designed to build on prior knowledge while introducing more advanced and applied skills relevant to future study and employment. The curriculum supports the school’s priority to equip students with transferable digital skills, critical thinking abilities, and an understanding of ethical technology use in a rapidly changing world.

description.value: Students will investigate, design, and prototype a specialised digital experience within a Minecraft environment, addressing a specific real-world problem. Students decompose the problem into manageable components, developing user stories and design criteria to guide their development. They will generate, communicate, and evaluate alternative design iterations, selecting and utilising emerging digital features and advanced tools to create interactive content for a diverse audience. Throughout the project, students apply agile project management techniques to plan tasks, manage risks, and monitor progress. The final submission requires students to evaluate their implemented solution against the established design criteria and user stories, while critically reflecting on potential future impacts and enterprise opportunities provided by the digital system.

conditions.value: 4–6 A3 pages or equivalent digital media pages that may include annotated graphical representations

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 10 students develop and modify innovative digital solutions, decompose real-world problems, and critically evaluate alternative solutions against stakeholder elicited user stories. Students acquire, interpret and model complex data with databases and represent documents as content, structure and presentation. They design and validate algorithms and implement them, including in an object-oriented programming language. Students explain how digital systems manage, control and secure access to data; and model cyber security threats and explore a vulnerability. They use advanced features of digital tools to create interactive content, and to plan, collaborate on, and manage agile projects. Students apply privacy principles to manage digital footprints.

lessons.title: Introduction to User-Centred Design (UCD) in Digital Environments
lessons.learningGoal: Define the core principles of User-Centred Design (UCD) and classify interface elements based on user accessibility and needs.

orientate.smartStart: Students complete a 3-minute quick audit on the board comparing an unlabelled generic software tool with a customised user-friendly dashboard, writing down one barrier a novice user faces.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can define the core principles of User-Centred Design (UCD) and explain how interface features solve specific user needs

activities.title: UCD Core Terminology Matching
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the four fundamental concepts of UCD: Empathy, Accessibility, Usability, and Iteration. Model matching the term 'Usability' to its formal definition on the main projector using the think-aloud strategy.
activities.studentsDo: Match the 4 core UCD terms in the workbook table to their correct definitions using the provided definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the definition bank in your workbook. Write the correct definition letter (A, B, C, or D) in the Match column next to each UCD term.
activities.questioning: Why is empathy considered the foundational phase of UCD rather than immediate technical coding? Expected: Because developers must understand the end-user's frustrations and operational context before writing solutions. How does accessibility differ from general usability? Expected: Usability is how easily any user can achieve a goal, whereas accessibility ensures users with diverse physical, sensory, or cognitive needs can access the system.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions: Usability (the measure of how easily and effectively a user can achieve their goal in an interface); Accessibility (designing systems usable by people with the widest possible range of abilities); Empathy (understanding the user's emotions, constraints, and experiences); Iteration (repeating a cycle of design, testing, and refinement).
activities.eLearning: Project the slide containing definitions while monitoring student focus across the classroom.
activities.transition: Now that we have established our core vocabulary, open your guided notes page as we examine how these principles operate in real community websites.

lessons.title: User Experience (UX) Flow & Environmental Cues in Minecraft

activities.title: Affordances and Signifiers in Game UI
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define the distinction between affordances (the functional properties that determine how an object can be used, such as a door opening or a lever activating a circuit) and signifiers (perceptual cues communicating where an action should take place, such as an illuminated pathway, contrasting block textures, or floating particle effects). Model the sorting process using an example: 'A pressure plate physically triggers a Redstone output, making it an affordance, whereas a glowing sea lantern above a dark doorway acts as a signifier guiding the player's line of sight.' Direct students to examine the scrambled bank in their workbooks and accurately categorise each Minecraft element into the appropriate bucket.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's modelling of environmental psychology concepts, take notes on the definitions of affordances versus signifiers, and complete the sorting task in the workbook by moving each scrambled game element into the correct bucket.
activities.visibleInstructions: Sort each Minecraft feature from the bank into either the 'Affordances' bucket (functional capabilities) or the 'Signifiers' bucket (perceptual cues indicating action).
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why do novice players frequently miss interactable wooden buttons placed on oak wood walls?
expected: Low visual contrast between the button and the wall creates a weak signifier, failing to draw the player's attention to the underlying interaction affordance.
prompt: How can dynamic lighting effectively guide a user through a virtual space without relying on text signs?
expected: Humans naturally navigate avatars toward illuminated focal points, leveraging high-contrast lighting to subconsciously direct user flow.
activities.scaffolding: Affordance: The actionable properties between an actor and an object (e.g., pressure plate activates Redstone, door swings open, chest opens an inventory grid). Signifier: Any sensory indicator that signals what to do and where to interact (e.g., sea lantern lighting a doorway, contrasting stone path on grass, signpost with directional text).
activities.eLearning: Laptops remain shut during teacher modelling of environmental psychology and UI design principles.
activities.transition: Transition to your workbook user flow diagram as we map the precise pathway an end-user takes from arrival to goal completion within a virtual environment.

activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach key Agile terminology using direct instruction and projector display. activities.questioning:
question: Why is an iterative Agile approach preferred over a traditional waterfall model when designing a digital solution?
expectedAnswer: Because user requirements and technical needs often change during development, allowing regular adjustments rather than waiting until the end.
question: What happens if a project team lacks a clear 'Definition of Done' during a sprint?
expectedAnswer: Tasks may be marked complete prematurely, leading to bugs, broken mechanics, or low-quality features.
activities.scaffolding:
Agile: An iterative approach to project management that builds software incrementally.
Sprint: A set period (e.g., 2 weeks) during which specific work must be completed.
Product Backlog: A prioritized list of features and requirements needed for the project.
Definition of Done (DoD): A clear checklist of criteria that must be met before a task is considered finished.

activities.title: Understanding the MoSCoW Prioritisation Framework
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model the MoSCoW method (Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have) using a sample St Brendan's College digital project on the projector screen. Demonstrate how to evaluate competing user stories against strict resource and time constraints, applying QCAA curriculum standards for project scope management.

activities.visibleInstructions: Listen to the demonstration and write down the key defining rule and operational constraint for each of the 4 MoSCoW categories.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the critical risk if a development team categorises every single user story as 'Must Have'?
expected: The project scope becomes unrealistic, risks overrunning the delivery deadline, and core functionality may fail due to resource exhaustion.
question: How does a 'Won't Have (this time)' classification actively assist with project scope management during a sprint?
expected: It explicitly sets boundaries so the development team avoids scope creep and does not waste valuable time on non-essential features during current sprints.
activities.scaffolding: Must Have: Non-negotiable core functionality required for the product to function. Should Have: Important features that are not vital for the initial release. Could Have: Desirable enhancements included only if time and resources permit. Won't Have: Agreed out-of-scope items for the current release cycle.

activities.title: Defining Software Validation & DoD
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher presents the definitions of 'Validation' versus 'Verification' in software engineering. Verification checks 'Did we build the system right?' while Validation checks 'Did we build the right system for the user?'. Introduce the 'Definition of Done' (DoD) as a quality gate used in Agile development to ensure a feature is complete and production-ready. Model an example: 'If we test that a redstone circuit triggers a door, that is verification; if we test that the player can safely escape a trap as intended by the user story, that is validation.'
activities.studentsDo: Students listen to the direct instruction on software quality gates, examine the technical definitions, and complete the matching table in their workbooks by linking the software terms to their correct definitions.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the technical definitions of software quality terms presented on the board. Complete the matching table in your workbook by pairing each software term with its correct definition letter.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the primary difference between verification and validation in software engineering?
expected: Verification is checking if the system complies with technical specifications, whereas validation is checking if the software meets the actual user needs and solves their real-world problem.
question: Why is a 'Definition of Done' (DoD) important before presenting a product to a client?
expected: It ensures a consistent standard of quality, verifying that all tests have passed, documentation is complete, and the solution is fully functional and free of game-breaking bugs.
activities.scaffolding:
The teacher provides the following core definitions on the board:
- Verification: Process of checking that software meets technical specifications ('Did we build it right?').
- Validation: Process of checking that software meets user needs and solves the real-world problem ('Did we build the right thing?').
- Definition of Done (DoD): A shared checklist of criteria that must be met before a project component is marked complete.
activities.eLearning: Projector displays key software engineering definitions and differentiation examples.
activities.transition: Now that we know the theory behind validation and the Definition of Done, let's look at how to construct a formal audit checklist for our Minecraft Experience.

activities.title: Core Privacy Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce key concepts around the Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) and data collection. activities.questioning:
question: Why is an online alias or gaming username considered Personally Identifiable Information under Australian law if it can be mapped back to a specific player?
expected: If the alias can be combined with other system logs (like school emails or local network IP addresses) to identify a real student at St Brendan's College, it is treated as Personally Identifiable Information (PII).
question: What is the primary difference between active data collection and passive tracking?
expected: Active collection requires explicit user input (e.g., submitting a registration form), while passive tracking occurs automatically in the background (e.g., server logs tracking coordinate history).
activities.scaffolding: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is any representation of information that permits the identity of an individual to whom the information applies to be reasonably inferred. Privacy by Design means incorporating privacy considerations into the product design from the initial planning stages. APP 3 (Collection) governs how entities collect solicited personal information.

activities.title: Evaluating Future Impact
activities.teacherDoes: Analyze a case study where a custom simulation is developed for tourism operations at Keppel Bay Marina (e.g., boat safety and environmental preservation simulations). Model how to evaluate long-term design requirements by examining infrastructure costs, scalability constraints, and software adaptability. Highlight key issues around safety risks, system scaling limits, and hardware deployment costs using professional QCAA software engineering terminology.
activities.studentsDo: Examine the projected Keppel Bay Marina case study and complete the guided notes in the workbook by using the word bank to identify missing structural design considerations, scaling factors, and technical requirements.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the projected Keppel Bay Marina case study. Complete the cloze sentences in your workbook by selecting the correct terms from the word bank to define long-term design and scaling requirements.
activities.questioning:
question: If Keppel Bay Marina scaled this virtual training map to hundreds of marine staff, how would they adapt their user experience requirements?
expected: They would need multi-language support, automated progress reporting, and lightweight hosting solutions to run on low-spec tablets and devices.
question: What is the primary risk of failing to plan for hardware infrastructure limits when deploying educational simulations commercially?
expected: Performance bottlenecks, high latency, and incompatibility with client-side devices, reducing overall commercial viability.
activities.scaffolding: Provide structured cloze sentences with explicit word banks highlighting core design concepts: 'adaptability', 'sustainability', 'infrastructure requirements', and 'Keppel Bay Marina'.
activities.eLearning: Access the real Keppel Bay Marina website at https://www.keppelbaymarina.com.au/ to show the range of charter operations, providing physical scale context for the simulation.
activities.transition: We have analyzed how systems scale in industry contexts. Let us now construct an Enterprise Opportunity Statement for your own interactive digital prototype.

activities.title: Drafting the Enterprise Opportunity Statement
activities.teacherDoes: Explain the structural requirements of an Enterprise Opportunity Statement to position a digital project for commercial or social viability. Model how to link a custom software modification to a real local context using the stimulus website https://www.stbrendans.qld.edu.au/ as an exemplar client. Emphasize how to articulate client value propositions, scalability, and risk mitigation clearly using QCAA achievement standard terminology.
activities.studentsDo: Independently draft their Enterprise Opportunity Statement inside their printable workbooks using the structured 3-2-1 written layout, addressing target client value, scalability, and risk mitigation.
activities.visibleInstructions: Write your Enterprise Opportunity Statement in your workbook. Complete the three sections: Target Client and Value Proposition, System Scalability and Adaptation, and Risk and Unintended Consequences.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must an Enterprise Statement focus on the client's problem rather than just listing technical software features?
expected: Commercial and institutional clients purchase solutions to their specific operational problems, such as reducing onboarding time or engaging students, rather than buying code features alone.
question: How does addressing unintended consequences and risk strengthen the commercial viability of a digital project?
expected: It demonstrates rigorous evaluation and proactive design, reassuring external stakeholders that the digital system complies with privacy standards like the APPs and operates safely.
activities.scaffolding: Provide a structured three-section template with prompt questions for target client identification, value proposition, scalability, and risk mitigation strategies.
activities.eLearning: Keep the sample enterprise statement framework and the Livingstone Shire Council portal reference visible on the whiteboard to assist with structural phrasing.
activities.transition: Incredible work drafting your pitches. Let us wrap up and reflect on how this completes our custom development process.

workbookSpec.title: Enterprise Opportunity Statement
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the future impact and commercial viability of your digital system by completing the three structural sections below.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:

Section 2: Scalability=The system can easily scale by loading new structure blocks representing different boarding houses.
Section 3: Risk=Unintended consequence of screen time over-use / Mitigation=In-game command block logs off users after 20 minutes of simulation play.
